extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, engineers, policymakers, and students of political economy interested in machinery, industrial organization, and labor effects
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating the technical design, economic justification, durability, and social effects of machinery used in manufacture and transport; includes criteria for selecting motive power, expected economic life, and arrangements between masters and workmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justifiability of expensive machinery when time savings are critical
rubrics_metrics.description: When the importance of saving time would allow of great expense in any new machinery for its accomplishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: printing presses and rapid conveyance of news; the text argues that where time-savings are crucial, high expense on new machinery is permissible. Use the value of time saved (and the public demand for speed) as a primary justification for adopting costly machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design criteria for mail-conveyance machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Desirable to reduce the weight of matter to be conveyed with the letters and to reduce the velocity of the animal power employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by a proposed wire-and-cylinder system: use high pillars with a stretched wire, suspended cylindrical tins rolling on the wire, and an endless smaller wire moved at stations to pull cylinders between stations. Notes advantages (velocity, multiple daily deliveries, express despatches, possible telegraphic use) and acknowledges obvious practical difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of motive power — steam versus animal power
rubrics_metrics.description: Steam may be employed as cheaply at a quick as at a slow rate and thus has advantages over horse labour which becomes more expensive as speed increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From House of Commons report: steam promises higher ultimate speed, cheaper operation at higher speeds, safer and more controllable operation (less danger of 'running away' and overturning). Consider efficiency at required speeds, fuel costs, controllability, and safety when choosing motive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propulsion method suitability for special environments (e.g., underwater vessels)
rubrics_metrics.description: A vessel to be navigated below the surface cannot be propelled by any engine requiring the aid of fire; alternative propelling powers (e.g., condensed liquid air) must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For rare but invaluable applications (submersible vessels), select propulsion compatible with the operational environment even if the technology is experimental or expensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of natural forces and local materials — simplicity and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Where natural circumstances favour it (timber at elevation), apply machinery that uses gravity and local materials in simple, economical constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Slide of Alpnach: an inclined-plane slide built mostly of local pine without iron, employing water to diminish friction and simple signalling among workmen. Criterion: prefer designs that exploit local topography, minimize external materials, and keep construction and operation simple and economical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate displacement of hand-labour and enable worker adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of new machinery commonly drives out hand-labour and produces suffering; it is important that workers are aware of effects and enabled to foresee them to diminish injurious results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy/design measures: promote increased intelligence among workers, savings banks, friendly societies, and encourage diversity of employment within families to mitigate fluctuations in labour value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider pace of technological change versus social cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether improvements should be so perfect as to defy hand-labour immediately or be introduced gradually; quick transitions produce more intense but less permanent suffering, slower transitions may cause longer-lasting harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical examples (power-looms vs hand-looms) to weigh short-term intensity of displacement against long-term permanence; where competition is hopelessly immediate, quick retraining may be preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill requirements of new machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly created labour often requires a higher degree of skill than the displaced hand-labour; displaced workers may not be qualified for the new roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess need for retraining programs and time required for workforce to acquire necessary skills when estimating social and economic impacts of introducing machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants of physical durability of machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration of effective machine operation depends mainly upon the perfection with which it was originally constructed, the care taken to keep it in proper repair (particularly correcting shakes or looseness in axes), and the small mass and slow velocity of its moving parts; sudden changes of direction and blows are injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for minimal moving-part mass and lower relative velocities where possible; prioritize build quality and maintenance regimes (address looseness, wear) to extend working life. Engines producing power (wind, water, steam) tend to have long lifetimes under good maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic lifespan, payback expectations, and replacement timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Improved machines are usually expected to pay for themselves in about five years and to be superseded by better machines in about ten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers should calculate payback periods and anticipated adoption rates; decisions to sell older machines (even at reduced price) and build new ones depend on expected time to recoup capital and competitive advantage (example: replacing looms when new designs repay cost in three years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary-market effects and price competition from resale of old machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale of older machinery at reduced prices increases productive capacity and lowers commodity prices; purchasers of cheap used machines may profit more and drive down market prices, accelerating obsolescence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the effect of a vibrant second-hand machine market on industry supply, prices, and the effective useful life of machines (example: older engines sold at half-price enabling buyers to undercut prices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of machine value to changes in product/process requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in the nature of the work or product can render machines suddenly less valuable or obsolete (e.g., introduction of 'cut-up work' greatly reduced the value and employment of many stocking frames).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating investments, consider technological and product-process risk that could change a machine's applicability; allow for possible rapid depreciation due to product innovation or changed production methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for clear, fair contractual arrangements between masters and workmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to assign fairly to each tool or produced article its proportionate value, or lacking a distinct, simple, and definite agreement between master and workmen, causes serious hardship and misaligned incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote transparent terms (frame rent, pay rates, responsibilities), and dispassionate discussion of proposed regulations; examples show poorly chosen terms induced widespread misery and structural problems in trades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and organizational options: renting machines and sharing power
rubrics_metrics.description: Machines are sometimes let to hire and power may be rented; central production of power with measured distribution could change manufacturing organization (possibly enabling a return to domestic manufacture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: frame-rent systems, Birmingham's renting of stamps/dies and horse-power; consider technical feasibility of transmitting power without much friction to distances and mechanisms to register quantity of power used. Evaluate rent rates, expected recoupment time (e.g., frame rent that clears frame value in nine years), and social consequences of rent-based arrangements.
